explanations.answer: Kill them and devote them to destruction
explanations.explanation: That's the order. The LORD says, “Kill them and devote them to destruction. Do all that I have commanded you…” and it's a heavy one. I'm not going to joke about this part, friend. I'll just say it plainly and let it sit.

explanations.answer: Warn them and give them a year
explanations.explanation: No warning and no year show up in this verse. The LORD's order against Merathaim and Pekod is to kill them and devote them to destruction. A year might sound gentler, but the text doesn't give one. It's a heavy verse, so I'll stick to what it says.

explanations.answer: Capture them and bring them to Zion
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets marched to Zion in this verse. The order is to kill them and devote them to destruction. Zion does come up later in this passage, but not here. It's a heavy verse, so I'll stick to what it says.

The text says the opposite. The hammer of the whole earth "…lies broken and shattered!" (Jeremiah 50:23). A hammer lying broken isn't swinging anything. Babylon had been the one doing the hitting, and now it's the one on the ground.
You've got it, baker. Babylon, the hammer of the whole earth, "…lies broken and shattered!" Think of a tool that's cracked in half on the workshop floor. Nobody's picking it up to finish the job.

Yes, horror. The verse says, "What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!" That's quite a turn for a place the verse calls "…the hammer of the whole earth…" The same verse says that hammer "…lies broken and shattered!"

Light is a nice word, but it isn't what the verse says. Babylon "…lies broken and shattered!" and the word is "horror." Nothing in the line has Babylon shining for anyone. Even my cookies don't glow like that, and I've tried.

A refuge is a safe place to run to, and that's not the word the verse uses for Babylon. After the hammer lies broken and shattered, the word is "horror." The verse says Babylon has become a horror among the nations. That's a very different picture from a refuge.
Right. God says, "You were found and captured because you challenged the LORD." The snare isn't random. The text gives the reason, and it's Babylon challenging Him.

explanations.answer: Because her walls were too low
explanations.explanation: This verse says nothing about walls, high or low. It gives one reason: "You were found and captured because you challenged the LORD." The text points to the challenge, not to the height of anything.

explanations.answer: Because her king broke a treaty
explanations.explanation: No treaty is mentioned here. The verse says Babylon was caught "…because you challenged the LORD." It doesn't mention her king in connection with the snare at all. The reason it gives is the challenge to the LORD.

Yes, baker. Here is what the verse says: "The LORD has opened His armory and brought out His weapons of wrath…" The verse also says this is the work of the Lord GOD of Hosts in the land of the Chaldeans. The armory is His, the weapons are His, and the work is His.
Trumpets of warning don't appear in this verse. What comes out of the armory is "…His weapons of wrath…" The verse says the armory is open and the weapons are out.

No gold is mentioned in this verse. The LORD opens His armory and brings out "…His weapons of wrath…" I'm a little relieved, because I keep my gold base for standing on. The verse is about weapons, not wages.
The text says the opposite. The orders say, "Devote her to destruction; leave her no survivors." (Jeremiah 50:26). It's a heavy line, and I won't dress it up. The word is no survivors, not a few.
That's right. The order is to "Devote her to destruction; leave her no survivors." There's no room for a few survivors in that line. It's a heavy one, so I'll just say it straight.

explanations.answer: The vengeance of the LORD for His temple
explanations.explanation: That's it. The fugitives and refugees are "…declaring in Zion the vengeance of the LORD our God, the vengeance for His temple." They've gotten out of Babylon, and what they carry into Zion is a declaration about the LORD. It isn't about themselves.

explanations.answer: The kindness of the king of Babylon
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have them saying that. What they declare in Zion is "…the vengeance of the LORD our God, the vengeance for His temple." Babylon's king isn't praised anywhere in the verse. Their message is about the LORD.

explanations.answer: A plan to rebuild Babylon's walls
explanations.explanation: There's no rebuilding in this verse. The refugees are declaring "…the vengeance of the LORD our God, the vengeance for His temple." They've left Babylon, and they're not drawing up blueprints for it. What they carry into Zion is a message about the LORD.
Yes, deeds. The order is, "Repay her according to her deeds; do to her as she has done." The verse says she has defied the LORD, the Holy One of Israel. The repayment is measured by what she did.
Wealth doesn't appear in this verse. The order is to repay her "…according to her deeds…" It's what she did that sets the measure, not what she owns.
Years aren't counted in this verse. The order is to "Repay her according to her deeds; do to her as she has done." Nobody is adding up birthdays here. The measure is her deeds.
Right, friend. The verse says, "The arrogant one will stumble and fall with no one to pick him up." He falls, and no one picks him up. It's a hard picture, and I think that's the point of it.
The verse doesn't name any officials. It says the arrogant one will fall "…with no one to pick him up." No one means no one, friend, even somebody in a fancy robe. It's a lonely spot to be in.
Egypt isn't mentioned in this verse. God says the arrogant one will stumble and fall "…with no one to pick him up." The verse names no allies, from Egypt or anywhere else.
True. God says, “And I will kindle a fire in his cities to consume all those around him.” It's right there in the verse. He speaks of cities, and the fire reaches those around him.
The verse says it plainly. God says, “And I will kindle a fire in his cities to consume all those around him.” So God does say it. It's a heavy line, and I'll leave it as it stands.

Yes. "Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of Hosts is His name." The verse before it says their captors hold them fast and refuse to release them. Right after that, the text puts the strength on the Redeemer's side. Israel and Judah aren't left with only their own muscle.

The verse doesn't call their army strong. It says, "Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of Hosts is His name." Israel and Judah are oppressed, and the text points them to the Redeemer. It doesn't point them to their own soldiers.

Egypt doesn't appear in this verse. The strong One is "their Redeemer," and His name is the LORD of Hosts. I've had friends promise to help me move a heavy oven, and the oven is still where it was. The text puts the strength on the Redeemer.

That's the word. He will plead their case "…so that He may bring rest to the earth, but turmoil to those who live in Babylon." Rest goes to the earth, and turmoil goes to Babylon's residents. The verse sets those two side by side.
Comfort doesn't finish this line. The verse says rest comes to the earth, "…but turmoil to those who live in Babylon." That "but" is a turn, friend. The word for Babylon's residents is turmoil.

No riches are handed out in this verse. The LORD brings "…rest to the earth, but turmoil to those who live in Babylon." The word that finishes the line is turmoil. The line sets rest for the earth beside turmoil for Babylon's residents.
The text says the opposite, friend. "A sword is against her false prophets, and they will become fools." (Jeremiah 50:36) The word is fools, not wise. So this one is False.
Right. The verse says, "A sword is against her false prophets, and they will become fools." The word is fools, not wise. That's why this one is False.

Yes. "A sword is against her warriors, and they will be filled with terror." These are the fighters, the ones who are supposed to be steady. The verse says terror fills them. The same verse has a sword against her false prophets too.

Courage is the opposite of what the verse says. "A sword is against her warriors, and they will be filled with terror." Warriors usually get a pep talk, but this verse doesn't give them one. Terror is what fills them.
Pride doesn't fill them in this verse. "A sword is against her warriors, and they will be filled with terror." The warriors aren't strutting around here. The word is terror.

Yes, plundered. "A sword is against her treasuries, and they will be plundered." What was stored up gets taken. The same verse also has a sword against her horses and chariots. It's the opposite of a savings plan working out.

Guarded isn't the word. The verse says the treasuries "…will be plundered." A sword is against them, so they don't stay safe behind a lock. I keep my cookie jar guarded, but this verse isn't about that.
The treasuries aren't getting filled. "A sword is against her treasuries, and they will be plundered." Plundered means things are taken out, not put in. The verse moves in the other direction.

explanations.answer: It is a land of graven images
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the verse gives. "A drought is upon her waters, and they will be dried up. For it is a land of graven images, and the people go mad over idols." The text ties the drought to the images and the idols. It doesn't give any other reason here.

The Sabbath isn't mentioned in this verse. The reason given is, "…it is a land of graven images, and the people go mad over idols." The drought comes with that reason attached. I'll stick to the one the text gives.

Nothing in this verse says the people mocked prophets. The text says, "…it is a land of graven images, and the people go mad over idols." That's the reason sitting right next to the drought. I won't add a different one.

Yes. The LORD says, "As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah along with their neighbors, no one will dwell there; no man will abide there." The comparison is about the place staying empty. Those two cities are the picture the LORD chose.
Jericho and Ai aren't the cities named in this verse. The LORD names "…Sodom and Gomorrah along with their neighbors…" That's a different pair. The verse says no one will dwell there.

Tyre and Sidon aren't the cities named here. The verse says, "As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah along with their neighbors…" Those are the two the LORD points to. It's an easy pair to mix up when so many city names float around in the prophets.

Yes, great. The verse says, "a great nation and many kings are stirred up from the ends of the earth." Notice it's a great nation plus many kings. The verse also says an army is coming from the north. That's a lot of folks heading Babylon's way.
The verse says great, not small. "a great nation and many kings are stirred up from the ends of the earth." Nobody's tiptoeing in with a little group. That's a big crowd, and it comes from far away.
Poor isn't the word here. The verse says a "…great nation and many kings…" are stirred up. Nothing about money is mentioned in that line. The text only tells us the nation is great.

That's it, baker. "The king of Babylon has heard the report, and his hands hang limp." The verse adds, "Anguish has gripped him, pain like that of a woman in labor." One report and his hands give out.
No sword gets grabbed. The verse says the king of Babylon heard the report, "…and his hands hang limp." Anguish has gripped him. A man reaching for a sword isn't the picture the text paints.
No treaty shows up in this verse. After the report, the king's "…hands hang limp." Anguish has gripped him. There's no pen and no paper, just limp hands.

Yes, friend, you got it. "Behold, one will come up like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan to the watered pasture." That's the spot the verse names. Then God says, "…in an instant I will chase Babylon from her land." I always picture a lion coming out of tall brush when nobody expected it.

The hills of Ephraim aren't named in this verse. The one who comes up like a lion comes up "…from the thickets of the Jordan to the watered pasture." The Jordan is the place the text gives. Ephraim isn't part of this picture.
Lebanon's forests aren't in this verse. It says the one who comes up like a lion comes up "…from the thickets of the Jordan…" That's the starting spot the text gives.
The text says the opposite. God says, "For in an instant I will chase Babylon from her land." An instant isn't a long time. It's about as quick as it gets.
Right. God says, "For in an instant I will chase Babylon from her land." That's quick, friend. Even a batch of cookies takes longer than an instant.
Yes, quake. The verse says, "At the sound of Babylon’s capture the earth will quake…" The quake belongs to the moment of that sound. The verse goes on to say a cry will be heard among the nations.
Singing isn't what the earth does here. The verse says, "At the sound of Babylon’s capture the earth will quake…" It's a shaking, not a song. I'd say that's more of a rumble than a tune.
Blooming isn't in this verse. The earth will "quake" at the sound of Babylon's capture. Nothing is sprouting. The ground is shaking.

True. The verse says, "At the sound of Babylon’s capture the earth will quake; a cry will be heard among the nations." The cry goes out among the nations. It's the second half of that line, right after the quake.
The verse says the opposite. It reads, "At the sound of Babylon’s capture the earth will quake; a cry will be heard among the nations." The earth quakes and a cry is heard, so the text includes both.
